note: Primary/deep construct: disentangles simulator sickness (SSQ), motion sickness (MSAQ/FMS), cybersickness proper (VRSQ), and discomfort as a separate ergonomic construct independent of VR content (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.2).

The review's own design: PRISMA-2020, PROSPERO CRD42024583656, PICO framework, 4 databases, 5423 records screened to 25 included studies (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.2-3).

note: Cybersickness assessed in 24/25 studies; 12/25 inconsistent/very-low scores, 5/25 high scores; discomfort minimal in 5/8 assessing studies (FE, p.14).
Oculomotor disturbances most-reported (9/25 studies), nausea second (4/25), disorientation moderate/high in 3/25 (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.14).

target: cybersickness & physical discomfort x desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
note: Cybersickness reported significantly higher for HMD than non-immersive VR comparator in 2/25 direct-comparison studies (Al-Khiami et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2020) (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.14).

target: cybersickness & physical discomfort x conventional instruction (control)
note: Andersen et al. (2023) and Elsenbast et al. (2024) each reported worse cybersickness for the HMD condition than the traditional-simulation control (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.14).

A type of visually induced motion sickness from mismatch among visual, vestibular and proprioceptive senses; not formally recognized as a health condition (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing McCauley & Sharkey 1992; LaViola 2000, p.2).
Originated in military flight-simulator research; measured by the 16-item SSQ across disorientation/nausea/oculomotor-disturbance categories (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Kennedy et al. 1993, p.2).
Range of physical/psychological symptoms tied to device weight, pressure, thermal regulation and restricted head mobility, occurring regardless of VR content (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Rupp 2024, p.2).

9-item, two-category (disorientation/oculomotor) instrument judged psychometrically better-suited to HMD VR than SSQ/SSQ-F, though used in only 2/25 included studies (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Sevinc & Berkman 2020, p.2, 15).
16 items, 3 categories, 4-point Likert; the most common validated cybersickness scale despite flight-simulator origin (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Rebenitsch & Owen 2016, p.2).
16 items, 4 categories, 9-point Likert; used in 2/25 studies (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Gianaros et al. 2001, p.2, 5).

Only included study reporting moderate-to-high scores across all three symptom categories (nausea, oculomotor, disorientation) simultaneously; HMD condition scored worse than the mixed-reality-mannequin control (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.14).

note: Huber et al. (2018) found cybersickness LESS prevalent in fully immersive VR (3.3%) than in augmented reality (6.6%), an explicit counter-case the review reports without resolving (FAITHFUL-Cossio, p.14).

SSQ was designed for flight-simulator contexts (fixed seated posture, non-stereoscopic image, no head tracking) and its psychometric properties are argued unsuited to measuring cybersickness in HMD VR applications specifically (FAITHFUL-Cossio, citing Sevinc & Berkman 2020, p.15).

target: cybersickness/novelty as substantive moderator of IVR learning <-> ignorable side-effect
note: (P/anticipatory-application) The review's own stance is measured, not alarmist: it documents genuinely inconsistent/low cybersickness scores in roughly half the 25 included studies alongside a real minority of high-symptom studies, and argues FOR taking cybersickness seriously as a reportable, disclosable moderator (educator disclosure duty, post-session driving risk) precisely because it has been under-measured as a secondary outcome — not that it is negligible. This unit anchors the 'substantive moderator' pole of Axis 7 with a mixed rather than uniformly alarming evidentiary base, a nuance to preserve when cited.

target: Part III dissertation (VR-HMD lab-condition disclosure & consent)
note: (P/anticipatory-application) This review's explicit disclosure-duty conclusion — informing learners of possible adverse effects, especially before post-session activities like driving — supplies a documented basis for informed-consent/debrief language in any HMD-based data collection Part III's lab pole conducts.

target: Part III dissertation (self-report symptom vs. behavioral confound caution)
note: (P/anticipatory-application) Because oculomotor disturbances and disorientation were the most commonly reported adverse effects and were assessed by largely non-standardized ad hoc instruments, any self-report attention/engagement/boredom measure collected immediately post-VR-session should be read against the possibility of confounding cybersickness symptoms.

target: ped-sec-10 (Makransky et al. - presence but less learning)
note: (P/anticipatory-application) Shared sensory-conflict/immersion-cost logic: ped-sec-10's finding that added immersion increases presence but decreases learning is a cognitive-load-side companion to this review's physiological-cost account of why higher immersion may carry a hidden price.

(P/anticipatory-application) CAMIL models presence/immersion as primarily an affective-motivational lever toward learning; this review supplies the physiological cost-side (cybersickness, discomfort) that CAMIL's own model does not itself operationalize as a moderator.

(P/anticipatory-application) Both are Strand-E systematic reviews of IVR-in-education literature; Radianti catalogues pedagogical affordances and applications broadly, while this unit supplies the adverse-effects dimension Radianti's review does not treat in comparable depth.

(P/anticipatory-application) Potkonjak surveys virtual-laboratory affordances for STE education without addressing cybersickness/discomfort as a constraint on HMD-based lab delivery; this unit's ergonomic-constraint findings are directly relevant to any virtual-lab deployment Potkonjak discusses that uses HMDs.
